Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.
  • Sources indicate that google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away.
  • But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Sources indicate that google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Sources indicate that cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

According to recent reports, “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the major questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really promptly.”.

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

Recent findings suggest that the resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the substantial selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” indicates Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”.

In a recent development, enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, notes Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he claims.

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

In a recent development, A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the upcoming papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Recent findings suggest that initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

Sources indicate that “All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he states. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”.

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the firm Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and  academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” notes Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the fresh studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important matter: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.

“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”.

Sources indicate that A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.

But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the firm accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”.

Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Recent findings suggest that yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the latest findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.

Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s key to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.

“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

#28432. How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6119 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
  • Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
  • According to recent reports, the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

According to recent reports, the Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

It has been revealed that in the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 highlights a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

According to recent reports, figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

According to recent reports, we’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Sources indicate that demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

In a recent development, at the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis indicates 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

Recent findings suggest that with the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

Sources indicate that we work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Sources indicate that figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

In a recent development, starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no newly introduced work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote fresh instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

In a recent development, shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut demonstrated that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to upcoming spectra.

Recent findings suggest that model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also indicates the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Recent findings suggest that our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

Sources indicate that such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

According to recent reports, public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

In a recent development, access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

According to recent reports, similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

Recent findings suggest that A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

For example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Industry observers note that harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

According to recent reports, each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

Industry observers note that the SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

According to recent reports, however, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

Recent findings suggest that balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

It has been revealed that existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

Table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

Industry observers note that our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

Sources indicate that in a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

In a recent development, benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

What a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a newly introduced harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

Sources indicate that that is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask latest questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Sources indicate that consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 reveals the setup.

Industry observers note that figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

Industry observers note that table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

Sources indicate that for the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

The model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Sources indicate that we built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

The D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

Recent findings suggest that the original instruction.md highlights why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

In a recent development, figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:.

The shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Recent findings suggest that our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

In a recent development, it is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

According to recent reports, several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

According to recent reports, finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

In a recent development, A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

According to recent reports, harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

Industry observers note that when a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each new model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 indicates the raman-lab results for each model.

Figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

It has been revealed that inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

Sources indicate that reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The latest work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

Task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Industry observers note that environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.

Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each new task.

According to recent reports, evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Industry observers note that verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The upcoming work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

According to recent reports, HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

Recent findings suggest that no-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

In a recent development, rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

Terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Industry observers note that trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports Replica First Patching, which reduces downtime during minor version upgrades.
  • Replica First Patching helps you keep mission-critical Oracle workloads current on minor versions with less disruption.
  • We recommend that you connect your applications through the Primary Endpoint when you use Replica First Patching.

In a recent development, amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports Replica First Patching, which reduces downtime during minor version upgrades. Replica First Patching is available for Enterprise Edition DB instances. With Replica First Patching, you apply a minor version upgrade to a replica in the same AWS Region first while your primary DB instance continues to serve traffic, and then switch over to the replica when you're ready to complete the upgrade. If the replica is in read-only mode, you can validate the fresh minor engine version with your read traffic.

Replica First Patching helps you keep mission-critical Oracle workloads current on minor versions with less disruption. You choose when to switch over within the switchover window, for example during a low-traffic period. If you don't switch over within the window, Amazon RDS rolls back the replica to its original minor engine version. After the switchover, Amazon RDS completes the upgrade on the fresh primary DB instance. Amazon RDS then upgrades your other replicas, including your former primary DB instance, to the same minor engine version.

We recommend that you connect your applications through the Primary Endpoint when you use Replica First Patching. The Primary Endpoint is a DNS name that resolves to the current primary DB instance, so your applications reach the fresh primary DB instance after the switchover without connection string changes.

Replica First Patching is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. Standard pricing applies to the replica DB instance. To learn more, see Upgrading with Replica First Patching in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

#28429. A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing.
  • Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the tech giant’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.
  • According to recent reports, this thinking isn’t all that fringe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the tech giant’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

According to recent reports, this thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% mentioned some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

According to recent reports, thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

It has been revealed that you might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

It has been revealed that the gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

It has been revealed that but it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he noted models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Recent findings suggest that nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”.

In a recent development, it has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

Sources indicate that but consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a manufacturer warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

#28427. Industry News: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2343 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark.
  • Industry observers note that deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction.
  • It has been revealed that one way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark.

Industry observers note that deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes.

It has been revealed that one way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking. Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, strategy and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions.

Industry observers note that robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice.

We introduce RoboTrack, a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces, Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M, a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.

Recent findings suggest that roboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos.

It has been revealed that our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks.

Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two fresh point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results.

RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views.

In a recent development, roboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold.

Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data.

To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better.

RoboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks. Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers.

Industry observers note that RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around.

A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos.

These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare.

According to recent reports, note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols.

Recent findings suggest that why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric, which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos.

In a recent development, this is where MolmoSpaces comes in—our robotic simulation environment at Ai2. We extend its existing manipulation simulations to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. In each episode, a simulated robot arm picks up an everyday object, such as a cup, a plate, or a block. Two cameras record the interaction: one on the wrist and one at the robot’s base, rendered in MuJoCo. Using the simulator’s geometry, object poses, and camera information, we calculate each point’s position and visibility in every frame without human annotation and filter out static points on the background and the robot’s fixed base.

Sources indicate that the pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M for training. RoboTrack-15M has 3,000 videos from 300 simulated homes with 5,000 tracks per video, for 15 million tracks in total.

Data generation pipeline of RoboTrack-15M. Objects, indoor scenes, and robot grasps are obtained from MolmoSpaces. We use the simulator’s geometry and camera information to calculate point positions and visibility.

Recent findings suggest that we introduce two models trained on RoboTrack-15M, RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. Each fine-tunes an existing tracker on RoboTrack-15M together with its original training data. RoboTracker builds on AllTracker, a lightweight model with 17 million parameters, and RoboTracker-Warp builds on CoWTracker, a much larger model with about 1 billion parameters.

It has been revealed that we’re releasing both model checkpoints so other researchers can inspect and build on this work. RoboTracker-Warp’s weights are for noncommercial use.

Adding RoboTrack-15M improves scores on robotics benchmarks. Compared with the released AllTracker and CoWTracker models, respectively, RoboTracker improves RoboTrack-Bench by 0.8 AJ (62.6 to 63.4) and RoboTracker-Warp by 2.1 AJ (63.9 to 66.0), with gains of up to 1.2 AJ averaged across the three robotics benchmarks. On general video benchmarks, both models perform on par with their base models. Overall, RoboTracker-Warp has the highest AJ of the models we evaluated on four of the five benchmarks. The exception is DAVIS, where BootsTAPNext and CoWTracker score slightly higher.

According to recent reports, improvements from fine-tuning on RoboTrack-15M, for AllTracker (RoboTracker) and CoWTracker (RoboTracker-Warp). The robotics average is taken over RoboTrack-Bench, RoboTAP, and RGB-Stacking.

Results on RoboTrack-Bench by video source.

Recent findings suggest that breaking the gains down by source reveals where they come from. RoboTracker-Warp improves on every source by roughly 1 to 3 AJ, including the human footage from EgoVerse and Ego-Exo4D, even though RoboTrack-15M contains only robot arms. RoboTracker’s gains are smaller and come mostly from robot footage—clearest on DROID Franka and EgoVerse EVA.

It has been revealed that roboTrack-15M is the result of multiple iterations and experiments with our synthetic data. In fact, our first attempt didn’t bring any gain on RoboTrack-Bench. To find out why, we looked at a simple question: how far do the tracked points move compared with real manipulation videos? We plot this as a histogram for each version of our data and measure its distance from RoboTrack-Bench (figure below).

According to recent reports, how far points move in each version of our training data compared with RoboTrack-Bench, for third-person (top) and first-person (bottom) views. Distance is the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between the two histograms, with 0 indicating identical histograms. Kubric has one camera type, so the same clips appear in both rows. AJ is measured on the full RoboTrack-Bench.

The histograms made it clear what was going wrong. Our first version picked points anywhere in the frame, including walls, floors, and furniture, so most points seen from the fixed third-person camera never moved. To address this, we next sampled points only on the robot and the objects it handles, which brought the wrist view close to real video and raised the score. Interestingly, we found that Kubric had the same mismatch in the wrist view, which likely explains why it alone isn’t enough for the varied viewpoints of robotic manipulation. Finally, we moved points from the robot’s fixed base and mounting platform onto the moving arm, which brings our third-person view in line with real video as well and raises the ablation score to 63.0 AJ, 1.5 points above the Kubric-only control.

Our wet-lab pipeline for guiding the robot with point tracks from a single demonstration.

In a recent development, what does better point tracking mean for robotics? Many robotic systems have found point tracks useful as a compact representation of how objects move that can guide a policy directly. To see this in practice, we built a similar system for a wet-lab task: pipetting liquid from one vial to another.

According to recent reports, here, a robot arm picks up an electronic pipette, draws liquid from the first vial, dispenses it into the second, and returns the pipette to its holder. The task is challenging because the pipette tip has to line up with the vial opening within millimeters, and the robot needs to adjust to different layouts of vials in each trial.

In a recent development, following RoboTap, the robot learns the task from a single demonstration, which we record by teleoperation and split into steps. At test time, the robot compares what its camera sees with the demonstration and uses RoboTracker to estimate the motion required to align with the vial. Because the following motion runs without further feedback, the task only succeeds if that estimate is accurate.

We compare three ways of estimating where the vial has moved:.

According to recent reports, we ran each method on 20 layouts with the vials in different positions: 10 with a clear view and 10 with partial occlusion. Point tracking completed the full transfer in 17 of 20 trials, compared with 8 for object masks and 5 for optical flow. It succeeded in all 10 clear-view trials and 7 of 10 with occlusion, where the mask-based method succeeded only once.

According to recent reports, the other methods fail in different ways. Optical flow breaks down when the vials sit far from where they were in the demonstration, and masks can latch onto a similar-looking object or lose the vial when it’s occluded. Point tracking, on the other hand, follows the same vial object from frame to frame, so it handles both large moves and partial occlusion. These results suggest point tracking is a promising tool for precise robotic manipulation tasks.

Success rate of pipetting trials with each method, with and without occlusion (10 layouts each). A trial counts as a success when the robot completes the full transfer.

We find the trackers still struggle with long occlusions, finding points when they reappear, and following small objects against busy backgrounds. Training on RoboTrack-15M improves performance, but these failures remain a challenge for real-world use.

Our simulations also focus on picking up everyday objects. They don't yet capture the precise movements involved in tasks such as pipette handling. A next step is to simulate these tasks more closely and test whether training on their trajectories improves tracking during deployment.

RoboTrack gives us a way to measure these failures and generate training data to address them. We hope the benchmarks, simulation pipeline, and released model help others build trackers that robots can rely on.

AWS Network Firewall introduces automated Internet firewall in public preview
