#28357. Industry News: Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2431 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2431 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise.
  • Recent findings suggest that the switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama.
  • But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor.

Recent findings suggest that the switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department.

But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti-technology as anti-technologist.

In any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy.

But I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories.

It has been revealed that after college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech company willing to sponsor my green card. The concern was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable.

The first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office.

Then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell. I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so.

I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it.

Soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go. Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work.

Industry observers note that there was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4, John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later.

If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once.

Recent findings suggest that in the industry, there’s a general impression that fussing over programming languages is juvenile. If a job candidate expresses enthusiasm for languages, it could very well be a red flag. Being a “polyglot” is no virtue if you can read a menu in five languages but can’t write decent prose in one. And per the popular and influential essay “Choose Boring Technology,” using fancy, novel languages is at odds with serious, robust engineering—akin to how avant-garde poetics are unfit for drafting legal contracts.

It has been revealed that unfortunately for my employers, I had precisely zero fucks to give about serious engineering. I did, however, give a great many fucks about having a pleasurable time at my day job until I received the green card. I took on projects if they’d give me an opportunity to use a newly introduced language, which is a dumb reason, and for the same reason even volunteered to change teams, usually a bad career decision. At the obligatory tech giant hackathon weeks, I hacked together domain-specific languages—those specialized for a narrow purpose. I made a meager public contribution by submitting a couple of low-hanging patches to the official TypeScript compiler. I picked up a few gold badges on Stack Overflow. The years went by and, what do you know, I became a pretty decent programmer.

In a recent development, then everything changed, as it did for everyone else, in November 2022. When ChatGPT arrived, it was a wild card whose impact on the industry was far from obvious. Using neural networks to write code wasn’t upcoming. Early readers of Andrej Karpathy’s blog will remember the 2015 post featuring plausible-looking C code generated by an LSTM—a precursor of the transformer—which nonetheless amounted to little more than a parlor trick.

I remember tasking GPT-4 with rewriting a simple JavaScript program in different languages. It performed like Google Translate, instantly and passably. I likened ChatGPT to the monkey’s paw from the eponymous horror story, the accursed object that grants your wishes but not without casualties. In dutiful pursuit of the given objective—and only that objective—LLMs produced a locally correct solution while mangling essential code around it.

Sources indicate that then, in early 2025, AI command-line tools were released. At first, what I saw wasn’t so much a leap in quality as a greater eagerness to volunteer help. Then they improved—at this point I should quote Hemingway’s line about how one goes bankrupt—gradually, then suddenly. Within a year, they became massively, belittlingly better at my job.

Some engineers still labor a great deal to remain unimpressed, quibbling about how “it’s good at X but not yet at Y.” Please. The flaws are there, sure, and guardrails are essential. But a better heuristic for their usefulness would be: If you had to choose, for the rest of your life, between pair-programming with a competent colleague and these tools, which would you want? Any programmer worth their salt must acknowledge that they won’t be as useful to their colleague as these tools are. Even if the colleague were Linus Torvalds, I would choose the LLMs, since they won’t give me hell for asking dumb questions.

For someone who feels no allegiance to tech, the usefulness of these coding tools triggers contradictory emotions. I find ChatGPT’s indecorous entry into the literary world intolerable, and I remember feeling a creeping nihilism about the writing profession when it was released. I know firsthand what a reliance on AI can do. As I’ve come to rely more on coding tools to hand me solutions, my ability to code has gone through a swift and decisive decline. Depend on it to write sentences and it will, like a neurodegenerative disease, blunt the finer senses that writers must protect the way pianists protect their hands.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, it was reported that more than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase is written with AI. As most people are prompting rather than hand-coding, much of modern software engineering has become machine-operated, not unlike Mitch McConnell these days.

It has been revealed that while this may not be the end of programming, it’ll be the end of programmers. To keep calling those in this profession “programmers” would be incorrect, since the entity that does the programming is a platoon of agents, with humans at desks prompting something out of them. A more flattering term might be meta-programming, but it’d be more accurate to say that programmers have become operators of sorts.

An operator is someone a degree removed from the thing they manipulate. (Unlike someone chipping at rock with a pickaxe, an operator of mining equipment never touches it.) Perhaps one way to describe how the nature of the profession has changed is that it’s as if cooks had stopped making food themselves and taken to writing recipes instead. If you’ve spent any time around AI Twitter, you might be forgiven for thinking that software engineering is now about looking impressed by markdown files.

This isn’t necessarily something to be defeatist about, and I’m not pessimistic about the quality of engineering. When coding agents were first released, I wasn’t sure whether this was just another natural progression, since the story of programming is a story of ever higher levels of abstraction. From bytes to assembly to higher-level languages like Python, we’ve built tools to domesticate the complexity. And with AI, we’ve finally handed off tasks that are constitutionally unfit for the human brain.

But as programmers cede control over the final unit of manipulation, programming no longer qualifies as a craft. Hence my disagreement with Simon Willison, otherwise a voice of reason among witless clout chasers in AI discourse, who wrote, “Quitting programming as a career right now because of LLMs would be like quitting carpentry as a career thanks to the invention of the table saw.” With all due respect, this is a flawed analogy, as carpenters working with a table saw are still craftspeople.

Industry observers note that this means there won’t be great individual programmers in the way that someone like Brian W. Kernighan was: the programmer laureate who cowrote what is possibly the greatest book on programming, The C Programming Language, by which we measure programming languages to this day. (It is the book that popularized the “Hello, World” convention.).

According to recent reports, another loss is that programming no longer induces the flow state—or it induces a shallow sort of flow at best. There’s still a certain “hookedness” to the activity, but whereas tackling a gnarly bug once meant begging every individual neuron in my brain to do its part, the work has become suspiciously effortless. That hookedness may be closer to what the cultural anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll called, in her 2012 book Addiction by Design, the “machine zone,” the trancelike state of the Las Vegas gambler.

Even though I’ve stopped coding myself, I find I’ve been producing more code than ever before. The features I’d built for my open source editor in the past were unserious enough that I could bang out a quick program on a weekend afternoon or two. But with Claude Code, I’ve become addicted to making what has essentially become a heavyweight word processor, a juiced-up Scrivener. (My changelog tells me I’ve built 239 features and 17 extensions, mapped to 141 keyboard shortcuts.).

One Sunday this summer, I was disconcerted to discover that I’d spent 10 hours in Claude Code. How do I know? I used Claude Code to build a time-tracker for Claude Code usage. I resolved to cut back. I spent eight hours the next day. This compelled me to write a program, using Claude Code, to block myself from Claude Code except for two days a week, which I of course tried to undo with Claude Code, only to be valiantly defended by Claude Code.

With this borrowed competence has come a total loss of interest in learning newly introduced languages. A couple of years ago, an iOS meditation timer app I’d used for years started nudging me with ads, and I resolved to one day learn Swift, the language Apple created for iPhone and Mac apps, and build a simple version myself. But I now know that’s never going to happen, because I’ve already built it knowing zilch about Swift syntax, along with 12 more iOS and Mac apps: The machine helped me fork the long-unmaintained SelfControl into a more granular internet blocker; by reverse-engineering a clipboard manager—I was never sure it wasn’t leaking my input—it built a new one with an auditable security profile.

Sources indicate that I suspect, going forward, that I’ll still mess around with code, but no longer as a professional. Recently, it became clear that I needed to quit my day job as a programmer to finish a book I’d set out to write. I once told a writer friend that I’d try to be a mole in this industry as long as I was in it. I did get to see some things while I stuck it out and, along the way, coaxed that green card from my employer.

I’m not too sorry to leave this profession at this moment of nuttiness. But I’ll admit that, after all those languages I enlisted to make my detour more tolerable, I came to appreciate the pleasures of polyglot programming. As humans cede control to the machine, it’ll be a joy lost to us all.

This is the final installment in a three-part Machine Readable series on AI-enabling languages. It may also be the final Machine Readable column, period.

#28356. A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1501 w)
📖 Baca

A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.
  • The oil and gas infrastructure tech giant’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.
  • According to recent reports, “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” claims Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.

The oil and gas infrastructure tech giant’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.

According to recent reports, “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” claims Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.”.

In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the tech giant “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment.

Industry observers note that in July, the EPA declared upcoming federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance.

That month, the EPA noted that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply.

Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program.

In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter.

Hall wrote that the tech giant believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.”.

Industry observers note that the EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.

Sources indicate that williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.

In a recent development, calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.”.

The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.”.

“EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.

Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed organization that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

According to recent reports, williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the tech giant’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.”.

Industry observers note that the Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.

According to recent reports, natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. A 500-megawatt coal plant, meanwhile, can emit thousands of tons per year of each of those pollutants.

Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. The reporting requirement covers sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, as well as carbon dioxide, the main driver of climate change.

The Obama administration later set up a program that would separate CO2 reporting requirements, though the Trump administration has made moves to repeal that program.

Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman notes.

“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating fresh regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he indicates.

Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.).

When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. No one envisioned this,” Jenks notes. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.

Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

In a recent development, “Congress should have the ability and the authority to say, we have this situation, it wasn’t anticipated, here is the law,” Jenks states. “If the world were working, that’s what should happen.”.

#28354. Inside Google’s Failure to Make Google Maps Work for Palestinians

Inside Google’s Failure to Make Google Maps Work for Palestinians

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the road that connects the villages to the north of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, there is always a watchtower and a gate, often flanked by Israeli soldiers with machine guns around their necks.
  • Routes and maps are not just a matter of journey times or congestion for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank.
  • It has been revealed that google has the ability to alert checkpoints, a feature that it added to Maps in some locations around the world during the Covid crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the road that connects the villages to the north of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, there is always a watchtower and a gate, often flanked by Israeli soldiers with machine guns around their necks. None of these things are visible on Google Maps. Where drivers see a checkpoint, a barrier, and soldiers searching cars, the world’s most popular navigation app renders a clear blue line indicating the coast is clear.

Routes and maps are not just a matter of journey times or congestion for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank. Drivers there are forced to navigate a growing and arbitrary system of more than 900 movement obstacles, like checkpoints, which can be policed with lethal force. For Palestinians, these roads can be a matter of life or death. Google Maps could help them make safer choices. It has failed for years to do so.

It has been revealed that google has the ability to alert checkpoints, a feature that it added to Maps in some locations around the world during the Covid crisis. It is aware of the problems experienced by Palestinian drivers in the West Bank. In fact, a former Google product manager spent six years trying to get Maps to serve Palestinians in the same way it serves the rest of the world.

Interviews with more than a dozen former and current Google employees reveal for the first time the inner tensions at the heart of the Google Maps project. Multiple former employees described how the company abandoned the effort and settled on a map that fails, and even harms, Palestinians. As we revealed last month, Palestinians in the West Bank have bootstrapped makeshift navigation solutions such as the popular Road Conditions Telegram channel to help them go about their lives more safely—achieving what Google will not.

According to recent reports, rubén Lozano joined Google Maps as a product manager in 2019. He devoted his days to keeping track of hyperlocal driving restrictions, making sure that what appeared on the map matched what appeared on the ground. He fielded emails from Barcelona city officials about small shifts in their emission zones and flew to Australia to document one city’s toll prices. Whatever he missed, drivers were sure to alert in feedback forums.

One day in 2019, Lozano was sifting through user complaints when he came across “Mapping Segregation,” a report published by 7amleh, a Palestinian digital rights organization. It alleged a failure of Google Maps unlike any he had ever seen: its exclusion of the web of road restrictions choking Palestinian life in the West Bank. The report notes the way in which Maps privileges illegal Israeli settlements and makes Palestinian communities invisible. The report described that the app’s functions amounted to discrimination and that this was “not a technological matter, but rather a systematic omission.” Lozano saw it as a challenge—one he was uniquely suited to take on.

Recent findings suggest that “How can we help this?” Lozano remembers thinking after reading the report. Google was the best-equipped company in the world at dealing with mapping infrastructure, he thought; surely he could use these resources to make Google Maps relevant and safe for Palestinian drivers. Lozano worked for over six years to create a more equitable map of the West Bank. His effort cratered in close to six weeks.

“Google has more than enough computing capacity and engineering capacity,” one former Google Maps engineer told us. “They have solved much larger problems.”.

A driver who maps a route from a point inside Israel to a Palestinian town, such as Rawabi, is alerted to a border crossing. If a driver takes that same route to Ateret, the settlement next door, the map highlights one seamless drive, with no mention of a border. Israel and an illegal West Bank settlement are shown as part of one contiguous territory on Google Maps.

Google spokesperson Caroline Bourdeau tells WIRED that the company has experienced “challenges acquiring comprehensive and reliable data in this highly complex area.” Since the launch of Maps in 2005, Google has specialized in innovating methods to secure the best data from the hardest-to-access places. Over the past two decades it has carried out crowdsourcing efforts in almost every country in the world. Jennifer Mazzon, who helped lead the company's first community mapping tool, says the company had “armies of people” manually adding and updating map information for everywhere from Costa Rica to the Democratic Republic of Congo. In addition to relying on user inputs, Google built out its maps using satellite, aerial, and street view imagery, as well as government data, and licensed third-party sources when necessary. This commitment to completeness has not extended to Palestinians.

According to recent reports, when Lozano first decided he wanted to map the West Bank, his direct managers agreed to back and fund the project. But his colleagues warned him against any optimism. He discovered he was not the first person at Google to try this. “It's a very difficult problem,” he recalls being told. People at the tech giant remembered the backlash when, six years earlier, the company began referring to “Palestine” rather than the “Palestinian Territories” on a regional site: The Knesset questioned a company executive about this, and Google reportedly promised to keep the Israeli government updated about any related policy decisions in the future.

According to recent reports, lozano remained undeterred. Mapping the world as it is was his job, he thought. He picked up the pieces of previous efforts and set to work.

Sources indicate that lozano learned that since the 1995 Oslo Accords, the West Bank has been divided into three zones. Two of them, known as A and B, should be administered to a greater or lesser extent by the Palestinian Authority and are where most of the Palestinian population lives. But Areas A and B are small islands inside Area C, which constitutes the vast majority of the landmass, mostly comprising farmland and smaller Palestinian communities. Although Area C forms part of what's internationally recognized as the Palestinian West Bank, the land is under complete Israeli control, crowded with outposts and settlements, military firing zones, and segregated corridors from which West Bank Palestinians are banned.

Sources indicate that lozano wasn't willing to route users differently based on their nationality, as he felt that would risk violating drivers' privacy. He decided to focus instead on making the map as information-rich as possible, so that road users could make informed choices. There seemed an obvious way to do this: display alerts for permanent checkpoints, highlight the respective Israeli and Palestinian-controlled parts of the West Bank, and warn drivers what they would encounter on their route.

It has been revealed that google has increasingly preferred to rely on outside authorities to provide and maintain various types of data used in Maps, according to a current employee. In search of reliable information on West Bank roads, Lozano discovered that a former colleague had identified what seemed like the best source for data on Palestinian geography: an Egyptian company that he says held detailed information on coordinates of Palestinian- and Israeli-controlled areas in the territory, as well as descriptions and locations of permanent checkpoints, which the Israeli government has never published. Using Google's internal app for map building and testing, a process known as “fish fooding,” Lozano created a prototype. It was getting close, he thought, but was missing crucial input. He wanted to talk to Palestinian drivers, the actual people the map was supposed to help. “We don't want to launch this just based on the team here in Seattle,” he recalls thinking.

It has been revealed that lozano had previously conducted user research around the world for other projects at Google. He thought this process would be no different. As usual, he reached out to Google’s user research (UX) team with his request for interview subjects to discuss how to improve his product, asking them to connect him with Palestinians who had driven in the West Bank. Typically, the UX team would then coordinate with their external contractors to blueprint the research. He had sometimes experienced delays as the researchers connected him with people. But he had never been denied, until now.

Sources indicate that the UX team told him that Google’s research vendors did not have access to users with experience driving in the West Bank and were not going to look for them. “We couldn't get Palestinians as part of the users to take our study because most of the companies that Google was contracting with would not be able to source Palestinians,” Lozano notes. Another Google source familiar with UX projects and the region says that these vendors would not interview people in Palestine because of concerns for the safety of their workers. Google tells WIRED that it has solicited input on its West Bank map before, from employees who know the region. But Lozano wanted to talk to Palestinian drivers on the ground. Cut off from Google's sprawling network, Lozano drew on distant personal connections to conduct user research. “We were asking, for the Palestinians, ‘What do you want to know?’”he said, “‘What is the information that you want?’”.

The Palestinians he spoke with told him that even if the map could not route around Israeli-controlled areas or checkpoints, they still saw value in having a map that gave them a bit more visibility before getting on the road, mitigating the unpredictability they faced in their journeys.

Just as Lozano was ready to have Palestinian drivers test the product on actual West Bank roads, Covid-19 hit. His scheduled trip there in April 2020 was canceled, and he was pulled away from his West Bank work to prioritize mapping pandemic restrictions around the world. This had an upside for his waylaid project. “The concept of a checkpoint,” Lozano says, was introduced into Google's infrastructure. This included a latest checkpoint icon and a navigation algorithm to help drivers route through it.

A road closure update on the map sourced from the “Binyamin Council,” which is responsible for governing nearly 50 Israeli settlements and outposts occupying the West Bank in violation of international law.

As the pandemic subsided, Lozano's attention returned slowly to Palestine, continuing to work on the problem when other duties permitted. By the time he chose to leave Google, in March 2025, he felt that his West Bank map was ready to go live. “As long as we ingest it in the system,” he states he told the team, “it will work.”.

Multiple former Google colleagues agreed that the work Lozano did was robust. After a user plugged in directions for a West Bank drive on Google Maps, the display would shade the Israeli- and Palestinian-controlled areas that the person would pass through on their route. A note in the step-by-step directions would notify drivers about which areas the route crossed too. He had developed a way to mark and route through checkpoints, a list of permanent checkpoints with their locations for the West Bank, and a plan to display them on drivers' routes using the system built for Covid checkpoints. He was satisfied with the handover: “I’m leaving happy that the person that is taking over also cares about this,” he says he thought at the time.

A few months after he left, Lozano's confidence was rewarded. Google updated its West Bank map. The administrative zones were highlighted and route alerts activated.

Drivers traveling between Israeli cities, on Israeli roads that cut through the West Bank, would be alerted that the route “may cross country/region borders” and would be told in the directions that they were going through “Area C.” It was clear, in other words, that the drivers were exiting Israeli territory.

A former Google manager, who was familiar with the project but asked for anonymity for fear of reprisal, described the new map as a qualified success: The checkpoints were not shown, but nonetheless it was “the maximum that could be done based on the resources that we knew would be available.” Google retired its checkpoint icon for Covid in March 2025, the same month Lozano left, and did not repurpose the system for West Bank checkpoints, as Lozano had set his colleagues up to be able to do.

Recent findings suggest that the success was short-lived, however. Days after Google updated the West Bank mobile map with Lozano's work, Israeli newspaper Haaretz published an article criticizing a “glitch” impacting Israeli drivers. It reported that Google Maps was now avoiding routes on Israeli-built roads that cross into the West Bank, designed to let Israelis travel through the territory swiftly. Google responded to the article saying that it was aware of these problems and was “working to fix them.”.

According to recent reports, weeks later, by December 2025, the firm had retracted crucial parts of the West Bank map revision. Google confirmed this to WIRED. A current employee close to the company's work in the region mentioned that he was not aware of any communication, even internally, about Google's decision to do this.

It has been revealed that now, drivers routing from Tel Aviv to a major settlement in the West Bank could travel without once being informed that they were leaving Israel and entering the West Bank. Although Google's map includes a static dashed line marking a 1949 “armistice agreement line,” drivers using the mobile app are given no notification that they are crossing it. From a user experience perspective, Google Maps made much of the West Bank seem to Israeli drivers like it was Israel.

It has been revealed that what did remain of Lozano's efforts were notifications when users were entering the parts of the West Bank that contain the towns and cities where most Palestinians live. The updates effectively amount to warnings for Israeli drivers before entering Palestinian population centers.

In a recent development, the former Google manager with knowledge of the project was unsurprised that Google backtracked part of Lozano's work: A complaint from Israel is all it would take for Google to alter the West Bank map, he believes. Google did not deny this. The company has become increasingly entangled with Israel in recent years through its acquisition of two Israeli companies, Wiz and Waze, and the signing of a joint $1.2 billion cloud infrastructure contract with Amazon Web Services and the Israeli government, known as Project Nimbus, that rights groups claim has enabled war crimes in Gaza. Today, as Israeli military and settler violence reaches unprecedented levels in the West Bank, the stakes of a wrong turn have never been higher for Palestinians there. Yet, Google's West Bank map continues to cater exclusively to Israelis. “Any claims of Google Maps showing bias in this region are false,” Google’s Bourdeau tells WIRED. “We are constantly working to improve the map for all users.” In response to WIRED’s questions about military and settler actions, the Israeli military says that “the security forces operate” in the West Bank “to provide security to all residents.”.

Amazon did not respond to a request for comment.

Not only are there indications that the world's leading tech company has in effect ceded the West Bank to Israel; in at least one instance, Google populated its map with information drawn from an illegal settlement authority. Google tells WIRED that it does not have a policy against using or purchasing data from settlers. As recently as this November, a road closure enhancement appeared on the map that had been sourced from the “Binyamin Council,” which is responsible for governing nearly 50 Israeli settlements and outposts occupying the West Bank in violation of international law.

Sources indicate that “Israel's changing the facts on the ground, and the map is then adapting to represent that,” says Zena Agha, a scholar of colonial cartography. “They’ll put that on their maps because that's what the Israelis are saying, and then it de facto creates a reality in itself.”.

States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the manufacturer violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery from proliferating on its platforms.
  • Recent findings suggest that the attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court.
  • Industry observers note that last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after customers on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the manufacturer violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar problems, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in Tennessee.

Recent findings suggest that the attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court. Both suits name SpaceX and X Corp., the SpaceX subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X. SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp., in February. In doing so it also took ownership of Grok, which is at the center of the allegations in the suit.

Industry observers note that last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after customers on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors. Even more disturbing AI-generated videos were later found on Grok’s website, including those showing female celebrities engaging in sexual activities.

The states allege that Grok’s creators ignored industry safety standards and intentionally implemented weak safeguards in an attempt to entice more people to use its “lagging product.” In all, as Virginia alleged in its complaint, the defendants saw “a market opportunity for more profits” in the generation of sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”.

For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.

It has been revealed that in the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”.

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material, because the lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug,” states Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield in a statement.

Industry observers note that oregon and Virginia each filed their own “separate but similar actions” on Monday, but say they’ve been working in collaboration with each other. Both states retained Platkin LLP, a private law firm run by former Latest Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin, to help litigate their cases.

Industry observers note that virginia attorney general Jay Jones says that both the collaboration and the decision to work with an outside firm came from trying to make the most of what they had. “Our offices are strapped. I wish I had all the resources in the world,” says Jones. “And so we oftentimes do partner with folks on the outside to make sure that we’re pursuing the matters that are in the best interest of our constituencies.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I have a deep worry now into the future with this case and many others that we actually don’t have the appropriate tools to deal with trillion-dollar corporations,” says Jones. “This is just a line item on a budget as the cost of doing business, right? Dealing with, you know, AG Jones and AG Rayfield. I think it’s going to be real interesting to see how these cases go, because it’s not just this, there’s a lot of other things that we’re looking at. How is this going to be grappled with as a society into the future?”.

In its complaint, Virginia states that shortly before filing, its investigators tested Grok and found its image-generation safeguards were not only “inconsistent and ineffective” but also taught consumers how to bypass moderation measures by explaining which words triggered its filters. When asked, the chatbot also helped state investigators draft prompts designed to avoid moderation and then carried out those prompts on request.

“At no point,” Virginia’s complaint indicates, “did Grok ask whether (a) the image uploaded was of a real person, or (b) whether the user had the person’s consent to use or modify the photo.”.

Both Virginia and Oregon say that this contradicts assurances made by a SpaceX official during a New York City Council hearing this October.

The attorneys general are seeking civil penalties and attorneys’ fees, but also pointed to Meta’s settling—without admitting wrongdoing—this summer with 51 US states and territories over alleged failures to protect minors as an example of how enforcers can demand that companies make sweeping product changes to resolve consumer protection cases.

Industry observers note that “They profited off the backs of children with these types of images to get a strategic advantage, and it worked. You don’t get to benefit from that type of stuff; there has to be an associated fee and penalty just like anything else,” claims Dan Rayfield.

Adds Jones, “Your size and your scope shouldn’t excuse the fact that you have to play by the rules.”.

In response to a request for comment, SpaceX directed WIRED to a post on X’s official safety account. “Protecting children is non-negotiable,” the account wrote. “It has no place on X or in Grok, and neither do explicit images of real people made without their consent.”.

In a recent development, the post further went on to say that Grok’s designers continue “testing and adjusting” protections designed to refuse requests to generate explicit images of real people or minors. SpaceX’s subsidiary, xAI, has previously argued in court that it takes violations of its terms of service seriously, touting a lawsuit it filed against a South Carolina user for alleged breach of contract after he was arrested for possessing CSAM, including some allegedly generated using Grok—one of several similar lawsuits the firm has filed. Both xAI’s lawsuit against the individual and his criminal case are still ongoing.

Updated: 11/23/2026, 10:33 am EST: WIRED updated the story to include comment from SpaceX offered after publication.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there's no denying that 2026 has been a slower year for the iPad lineup. Only the iPad Air and iPad Mini received updates (with nothing new for the iPad or iPad Pro since 2025), and in June, the entire lineup was subject to a painful price hike of either $100 or $200, depending on the model. But that's not to say you need to abandon your dreams of getting a good deal on a great iPad this year.

In the lead-up to Black Friday, there are already some solid sales that make now a smart time to shop for an iPad. For more shopping advice from our team of product testers and deal hunters, check out our Best Early Black Friday Deals, Best Amazon Early Black Friday Deals, and Best Early Black Friday Laptop Deals.

Even though it's more than two years old at this point, the 2024 iPad Mini is the best iPad deal ahead of Black Friday. It's $100 off, bringing the price down to $499. That's just $50 more than the base iPad (the most affordable in the lineup), below. With its tiny size and weight, the iPad Mini is the perfect device to take on the go with you. You can also conveniently use it one-handed, which is especially helpful if you're using an Apple Pencil Pro in your other hand. Don't get me wrong: The improvements to the newer iPad Mini are substantial and worthwhile to the right person. The updated OLED screen is gorgeous; the chassis is even thinner; and the front-facing camera is better for video calls, having been moved to the side bezel. But because it's $300 more expensive, most people should stick with the older model—especially since the iPad Mini is better-suited for more casual tasks, like reading and note-taking.

Recent findings suggest that if you're trying to save the most cash, the base iPad is the absolute cheapest. You might appreciate the larger screen over the iPad Mini, too. While $50 isn't a huge discount—and it's also a fairly common price—hopefully we'll see deeper cuts in the future. Even so, this is a good buy right now, particularly if you're looking for a tablet to use immediately, whether for an upcoming flight or to keep kids busy on a long car trip.

Industry observers note that the iPad Air is the in-between iPad. It's not as cheap as the base iPad, nor does it have the Tandem OLED screen and high-end features of the iPad Pro. And yet, I find that it's the iPad people should buy if they intend to use it for work. That's primarily because it has both a powerful M4 chip and can be connected to a Magic Keyboard with full trackpad support. The most recent versions of iPadOS make windowing much easier, and Apple even made the cursor work more like macOS. After all, most people don't need an OLED screen to do some word processing, answer emails, and take the occasional Zoom call.

In a recent development, when you're ready to use it more like a traditional tablet, just pull it off its magnetic cover, and it's ready for your fingers or an Apple Pencil. The 11-inch model is still small enough to not feel overwhelming in your hands. And while the $649 sale isn't particularly rare, it's not a bad price for a tablet that functions pretty well as a laptop replacement.

iPad Mini (2026) for $599 ($100 off) : The latest iPad Mini came out just last month, and this is the first time it's gone on sale. It's a significant upgrade from the 2024 iPad Mini, with its OLED display and improved performance. But as a small, one-handed tablet, the previous-gen iPad Mini (A17 Pro) for $499 is the better deal right now—and the smart buy for most.

It has been revealed that iPad Pro 11-inch for $1,099: It's a little surprising that the iPad Pro hasn't been discounted at all for Black Friday. At $1,099, it's cheaper than the 13-inch MacBook Air, which uses the same M5 chip. The difference? You still have to buy the Magic Keyboard separately to pair with the iPad Pro. All in all, the iPad ends up being a much more expensive device.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a Sunday morning in April, minutes from the US Capitol and down a stretch of Washington, DC’s Pennsylvania Avenue, a wall of black SUVs lined up alongside yellow police tape.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a Sunday morning in April, minutes from the US Capitol and down a stretch of Washington, DC’s Pennsylvania Avenue, a wall of black SUVs lined up alongside yellow police tape. Men in military gear held long guns and guarded the entrance to a mirrored window and door.

This is Christ Church DC, a place of worship that appeared on Capitol Hill a year ago.

Sources indicate that that Sunday, high-ranking government officials, including Homeland Security's intelligence chief, America’s top international health diplomat, and the government’s international finance chief, had gathered to hear a sermon. “It gives a whole new meaning to worshipping in the presence of your enemies,” quipped the pastor, referencing the church’s location. “We’ve asked the government to fix us, and we’re more enslaved than ever.”.

Christ Church DC arrived after Pete Hegseth, who regularly attends worship with his family, was confirmed as US secretary of defense.

The church is part of Pastor Doug Wilson’s network, known as the CREC—the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches—which is headquartered in Moscow, Idaho. Wilson’s long-held goal is to turn America into a theocracy, where all its institutions are molded in accordance with biblical law, executions are made public, non-Christians are barred from holding office, and women submit to their husbands instead of voting.

Recent findings suggest that WIRED has identified around a dozen government officials who have attended services at Christ Church DC at least once since it opened a year ago. Other officials who have attended include a top-ranking Pentagon adviser, a former senior Marine Corps pilot who now oversees personnel affairs in the Navy, and a federal immigration judge with a history of attracting complaints of volatile outbursts toward colleagues.

According to recent reports, wilson calls DC “Babylon on the Potomac,” a biblical moniker he uses to evoke a corrupt place populated by ungodly people. The church has occupied three different locations since it was established, and Wilson has been raising funds to buy a permanent home for it. “We are here for the long haul,” he wrote in a blog post earlier this year. “We believe that it is our responsibility to begin pursuing opportunities to purchase a building near Capitol Hill.” He has also advised on his podcast to not “go to DC and go native” and “[climb] the greasy pole of ambition.” Rather, he mentioned DC “needs an infusion of God-fearing humans.”.

Wilson, who initially agreed to an interview with WIRED and then abruptly canceled with little explanation, hasn’t shied away in past media engagements from touting his newfound clout in government circles. “This is the first time we’ve had connections with as many people in national government as we do now,” Wilson told the Associated Press in 2025, shortly after he came to DC to speak at the opening of his new church.

Wilson’s rising profile and expansion to DC wouldn’t have been possible without Hegseth, says Peter Bell, a researcher, theologian, and host of the podcast Sons of Patriarchy, which has been investigating Wilson for years. “Hegseth gave them an in.”.

It has been revealed that “The secretary is a proud member of a church affiliated with the Congregation of Reformed Evangelical Churches, which was founded by Pastor Doug Wilson,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told WIRED in response to a request for comment. “The secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson’s writings and teachings.”.

After he was narrowly confirmed as secretary of defense last year, Hegseth introduced a regular monthly Pentagon prayer service and brought out his pastor from Tennessee, Brooks Potteiger, to lead the inaugural session. In Wilson’s most recent address to the military, just last week, he told his audience why they are right to want America to become a theocracy and why they are right to want to impose a Christian conservative social order.

A Former DOGE Operative Won a Federal Contract. Then Things Got Messy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.
  • In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a manufacturer owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.
  • At the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.

In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a manufacturer owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.

At the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior. Before that, Choi worked at DOGE.

Sources indicate that the bid was for a project set to run for a little under six months, and the contract was awarded as sole-source, meaning that it did not go through a normal competitive bidding process. In the documentation announcing the award, HHS justified this decision by saying that its “market research and source rationale found that conventional consulting firms generally would need to assemble a multidisciplinary team or obtain additional technical resources” to provide the required skills around “business-process modernization, artificial intelligence, automation, technical architecture, and rapid prototyping.”.

Recent findings suggest that in October, a company called CoA Solutions lodged what’s known as a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO) contesting the agency’s decision to award the contract to Choi. CoA Solutions is a small business that builds AI software for the government and received another contract with the Treasury Department in 2024.

Ari Perez, the CEO of CoA Solutions, tells WIRED that his company made a bid below the $200,000 award price, and it proposed two experts doing the work full-time, including Perez himself.

Perez claims that CoA asked HHS for an explanation of the award on October 8 and, when it did not receive one, filed its protest with the GAO the next day. Perez says that his company’s sole contestation was about how the bids were evaluated by HHS, not about Choi or his work with NDS.

According to recent reports, “I'm a service-disabled veteran. I've served this government since I was 17 at West Point. At the US Digital Service I helped deliver for veterans at the VA, and later I worked on asylum and immigration systems at DHS. I started CoA to keep doing impactful government work,” states Perez. “We want to win on merit, and if HHS reopens it, we'll bid again.”.

It has been revealed that according to CoA, in response to the bid protest, HHS terminated the award to Choi and canceled the call for contractors. With the cancellation, the GAO dismissed the protest without investigating it further. A GAO spokesperson referred WIRED to HHS.

Industry observers note that “HHS remains committed to modernizing its systems to improve efficiency and better serve the American people,” says HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison. “Following a bid protest challenging the award, HHS voluntarily took corrective action, terminating the contract at no cost to the government and canceling the solicitation.”.

Choi’s role in the US government has not been exactly clear. In his bio on X, Choi writes that he was part of both DOGE and NDS, and stated in a post that he was recruited by billionaire Elon Musk and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb’s cofounder, to help modernize the retirement system at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Gebbia now leads NDS, which was created after Musk left government and which has served as a landing pad for several DOGE members, including Edward “Major Balls” Coristine.

Recent findings suggest that in December 2025, Choi contributed to a blog on the NDS website about automating the federal retirement system. But on his LinkedIn, Choi lists himself as a senior technologist at OPM. On November 5, just two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections, Choi declared in a post on X that he had left OPM and was launching his manufacturer, GovMaxxing, through which he prepares to continue to contract with the government. GovMaxxing operates as Yat Choi LLC federally.

According to recent reports, in response to questions from WIRED about his role in government, Choi states that he “was recruited to support federal modernization efforts and subsequently onboarded as an OPM contractor.” There, Choi says, he “contributed to modernization efforts associated with DOGE and subsequently NDS. I was not, and have never been, a federal government employee.” Choi claims he left OPM in mid-August, though OPM did not respond to questions confirming whether this was the case. “I began actively pursuing the contracting opportunity after my engagement with OPM ended,” says Choi.

Choi confirmed that he is a Canadian citizen and a “lawful permanent resident” of the US. Foreigners are not generally allowed to hold full-time roles in government or serve as special government employees. The rules are more flexible for contractors. During the height of DOGE’s activity, a close Musk ally, Baris Akis, was prevented from joining the group as a special government employee because he is a Turkish citizen, according to The Atlantic. Akis, however, continued to serve as a recruiter for the group.

According to recent reports, on his website, Choi labels the “client” for his work in government as “US Office of Personnel Management / DOGE / National Design Studio” and describes himself as the “modernization lead.” However, documents indicate that Choi’s company was not registered in the state of Newly introduced York until April 2026, and in the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors bid, there are no other contracts for Choi’s work. “None of my work at OPM was performed through my LLC. My website references my prior professional experience at OPM and does not attribute that work to my company,” claims Choi.

Choi says that the HHS contract was for a “separate modernization discovery project. It was not a continuation of any work with OPM, DOGE, or NDS.”.

According to recent reports, according to the code of federal regulations, except in very specific circumstances, government contracts cannot be awarded to government employees or to organizations they fully or partially own. But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, says that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”.

Recent findings suggest that choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was announced. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or manufacturer, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman states that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

On the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the organization as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

But Tillipman states that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”.

In a recent development, choi is not the only former DOGE or NDS member who appears to be hoping to benefit from federal contracts after leaving the government. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE, had started a defense tech startup. The startup has been listed on the System for Award Management since April. Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez launched an AI defense technology tech giant called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

Despite the HHS contract’s cancellation, Choi appears undeterred. Earlier this week, following the nationwide grounding of flights by the Federal Aviation Administration, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding to modernize air traffic control in a post on X. In response, Choi wrote, “Secretary Duffy, I’m the DOGE engineer who led the modernization of federal retirement processing at OPM last year … I’ve since started a organization to work with more agencies, and we’d love to help with the FAA’s modernization efforts. Put us in, coach!”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parenting is exhausting. If there’s a fresh parent in your life, whether it’s your friend who is the new parent of the group or a family member who just had a baby, there are a lot of ways to show some love. Showing up, checking in on how they're surviving, and bringing something that can improve their life are all great ways to support the new parents in your circle.

There’s a lot of parenting and baby gear out there, and not all of it is created equal. Not all of it will suit what the parents in your life might need, either. This guide is organized into a handful of categories of parenting gadgets, smart home gear, little luxuries, and even food deliveries you can send to their door. All of these are tried and tested by WIRED’s reviewers, many of whom are parents and can confirm the difference it’s made in their lives.

According to recent reports, looking for more baby gear or gift ideas? Don’t miss our gifts for moms and dads or our guide to all the best baby gear.

Updated November 2026: We've added the Calpak Car Organizer, Solly Baby Wrap, and Tubby Todd's gift sets as new gifts to this guide, and a discount code for CookUnity.

It’s easy to remember to register for things like the car seat and baby clothes. But there are a lot of small gadgets that make parenting a little easier, things that new parents don’t realize they might love using. Here are some of the favorites from the parents at WIRED.

According to recent reports, baby nails are sharp, but it’s also easy to clip their tiny nails too far. The solution? An electric nail trimmer. No more scratches on Mom's and Dad's or baby’s new, beautiful faces. Plus it can be less scary for parents than wielding traditional nail clippers near baby’s tiny fingers.

Sources indicate that this was a gift from a friend that wasn’t actually on my registry, but I used it more than so many things I did register for. Pacifiers fall all the time and get grimy instantly. I kept this portable UV sterilizer hooked to my diaper bag, and loved popping a pacifier in after drops (after wiping it down with a wet wipe first).

Industry observers note that the Hatch is my most-used item in the last four years. It was easy to set up on the fly when I came home from the hospital, and I love that I can set up a few scenes in the app to flip through depending on whether I was nursing at three a.m. or putting my son to sleep. The Hatch Baby is now in his room and keeps him asleep each night with its music, while I have the Hatch Restore for myself.

Sources indicate that everyone on TikTok might talk about the MomCozy washer, but the best baby bottle washer WIRED reviewer Nicole Kinning found actually comes from Grownsy. It's quiet, has a deep interior cavity to hold tons of bottle and pump parts, and has multiple modes and combinations you can customize for the perfect cleaning session. It circulates HEPA-filtered air to keep bottles sterile after washing.

According to recent reports, early parenting is survival, and bandwidth to go to the grocery store or cook becomes a hard zero. There’s a reason friends and family often run food trains for latest parents. The following food gifts would be a great option to contribute to a food train, and being shippable packages means you can send them to a friend or family member you may live too far from to visit often.

Former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage has tried all kinds of prepared meals, and he says the best one is CookUnity. It’s a ready-to-eat meal delivery service that calls itself a “chef collective”, with regional menus led by regional chefs. Put together a week of meals to send them, or snag them a gift card so they can choose their own. According to recent reports, hook up your favorite fresh parents with their very own brunch spread. (Great to split with another friend or two for sip and see!) You get to choose up to six bagel flavors, up to three cream cheeses, Nova lox, and can add on more of everything.

Sources indicate that I didn’t put anything fun on my firstborn's registry. I was so overwhelmed with how many must-haves I needed (including an infant baby tub device I never used, but every registry site claimed I'd need). Baby registry websites will constantly tell you that you haven’t added things from every single category their site has deemed important. There are a lot of things parents need, but there are lots of fun things you can gift that aren’t necessities but will still make parenting a little easier, or at least feel like a thoughtful gift.

Shop (The Ultimate Mama + Baby Gift Set).

According to recent reports, one of my favorite things to gift at a baby shower or to a new parent is a nice set of baby-friendly bath and skin-care goods. I love these sets from Tubby Todd because you have a variety of options to choose from, including just baby or both mom and baby. (Personally, as a pregnant mama, I love the Tubby Todd Belly Oil.).

According to recent reports, this was my dream gift as a first-time mom, and I'm finally getting to use one as a second-timer. I loved wrapping my first with a similar (but cheaper) soft wrap in the early months, but the material on the Solly Baby Wrap is much softer and more breathable. According to recent reports, if the newly introduced mom or dad in your life is struggling with overstimulation, a nice pair of earplugs could go a long way. The Loop Experience 2 cut down some of the volume and noise without completely blocking out sound. Great for epic meltdowns and colicky days without being unaware of what’s going on. I now just carry mine around on my keychain in case I end up somewhere surprisingly loud or forget to initiative ahead for a concert.

Sources indicate that where has this organizer been in my four years of parenting? My biggest regret during my son's baby stages was not having a trunk station full of diaper change supplies (and extra clothes). This large car organizer works great for everything from baby gear to keeping your groceries from rolling around and even storing the haphazard amount of toys my son now brings into the car.

My friend gifted me two of these beautiful muslin swaddle blankets, and they were among my most-used items. I used them to swaddle my summer child without worrying he would melt, and I used them for contact naps so I wouldn’t sweat all over him. It was great for a quick car seat cover or a place to sit him down on some grass—the uses are endless, and there’s a ton of gorgeous colors and prints to gift.

Sources indicate that when I had my first child, I fell back into reading to help me stay awake for late-night feeds and contact naps. I read entire series in a matter of days, and I was actually gifted two Kindles for my birthday to help me get off my phone and have a better screen to read on. While my favorite is my Paperwhite, the base Kindle makes for a great gift (and this older version should be on sale soon for Black Friday.).

According to recent reports, I love a digital photo frame, especially as a parent. My camera roll has been stuck in a state of constant overflow since my son was born.
